analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin costs at $35 a month for people 26 and under on private insurance plans.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap insulin cost-sharing for children at $35 a month was referred to three House committees and has not received a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require private health insurance plans — employer plans, individual plans, and even catastrophic plans — to cover insulin for anyone 26 or younger without applying a deductible, and to charge no more than $35 for a 30-day supply (or 25% of the drug's negotiated price, if lower). It amends the laws governing employer health plans, the Affordable Care Act, and the tax code so the rule reaches nearly all private coverage. It does not cap prices for adults over 26 or for public programs like Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, teens, and young adults 26 or younger who need insulin — and their families — would pay nothing toward their deductible and no more than $35 per 30-day supply for covered insulin, regardless of the type (rapid-acting, long-acting, etc.) or form (vial, pump, inhaler). Families currently pay full price for insulin until meeting high deductibles; this would end that for young people on private insurance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young people with diabetes on private insurance

how_it_helps.text: For plan years starting January 1, 2026, plans and insurers could not apply any deductible to covered insulin for people 26 or younger, and could not charge more than the lesser of $35 or 25% of the insulin's negotiated price per 30-day supply.

The rules apply across private coverage — employer plans under ERISA, individual plans under the Public Health Service Act, and even catastrophic plans, which would have to cover insulin before the deductible is met.
Plans must cover at least one product of each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) of each insulin type (rapid-acting, long-acting, and so on), so families would not be pushed onto a single formulation.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor plans would absorb the cost of covering insulin before the deductible and capping cost-sharing. Those costs would likely be spread into premiums. Insulin manufacturers' prices are untouched; the bill regulates cost-sharing, not drug prices.

drawbacks.text: The protection applies only to people 26 and younger, leaving adults with diabetes — the majority of insulin users — subject to whatever cost-sharing their plans impose, and it does nothing to lower insulin's list prices themselves.
Insurers and employers would absorb the cost of covering insulin before deductibles, which could show up as slightly higher premiums for everyone in a plan.

Plans choose which insulin products count as 'selected' products, so the protection is only as good as each plan's selection — a plan could pick cheaper insulin formulations and charge more for newer ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to young insulin users is direct and meaningful: no deductible and a $35 monthly cap on covered insulin can save families hundreds to thousands of dollars a year [S2]. The costs — slightly higher premiums spread across everyone insured, and some added compliance burden for employers and insurers — are real but modest relative to the medical harm that unaffordable insulin causes. On the whole, a well-targeted consumer protection, though its reach is limited to people 26 and under.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2025 and referred to three House committees, and no further action has been taken since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 3, 2025, and referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce committees.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since the referral.
The bill has 9 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost: insurers and employers keep charging full cost-sharing on young people's insulin, and no one has had to vote on the record about it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has simply stalled

for.name: Reps. Norton, Dean, McGarvey, Thompson of Mississippi, and Gottheimer
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce Committees
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral; none has taken further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has not moved in committees controlled by the House majority.

industries.note: Insurers could no longer apply deductibles or charge more than $35 a month for covered insulin for enrollees 26 and under, shifting those costs from families to plans [S2]. Many large employers, not just insurers, bear this through self-funded plans.
The bill's cost-sharing cap is calculated net of all price concessions, including those captured by PBMs, so rebate arrangements can no longer inflate what families pay for insulin [S2].
The bill regulates cost-sharing, not drug prices, so manufacturers keep their list prices; the burden falls on insurers rather than directly on drugmakers [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits with three committees and only Democratic support. Most House bills referred to multiple committees without a hearing or markup this early in a Congress never reach the floor; the realistic path would be inclusion in a larger health or drug-pricing package, which is not indicated by the record.
